title: Phones banned in schools

turns.speaker: Keisha
turns.text: Phones go in a pouch at the gate from September. Locked, handed back at three.

turns.speaker: Ollie
turns.text: Parents will hate it more than the students, I'd guess.

turns.speaker: Rhodri
turns.text: They do, consistently. The objection is always contacting their child in an emergency.

turns.speaker: Keisha
turns.text: Which is understandable and also the thing schools handled for a century with an office telephone.

turns.speaker: Ollie
turns.text: What does it actually change, though? I'd want to see something better than teachers saying it feels calmer.

turns.speaker: Rhodri
turns.text: The attainment evidence is mixed and modest. Where it's clearest is for lower-attaining students, who gain most.

turns.speaker: Keisha
turns.text: That pattern turns up everywhere in education research.

turns.speaker: Ollie
turns.text: So the average effect being small hides a real effect on the people who need it.

turns.speaker: Rhodri
turns.text: The bigger change reported isn't lessons at all. It's break time. The corridors get loud again.

turns.speaker: Keisha
turns.text: That's the part I find most convincing, honestly. Not the maths results, the fact that they talk to each other.

turns.speaker: Ollie
turns.text: The counter-argument is that it's a life skill. They'll have phones at eighteen with nobody confiscating anything.

turns.speaker: Rhodri
turns.text: True, but you teach swimming in a pool, not by pushing someone into a river.

turns.speaker: Keisha
turns.text: I'd want an explicit lesson on it rather than pretending the ban teaches it by itself.

points: A school will lock phones in pouches during the day from September.
Parental objections centre on emergency contact, which Keisha notes was handled historically by the school office.
Attainment evidence is mixed and modest overall, with the clearest gains among lower-attaining students.
Ollie observes a small average effect can conceal a meaningful effect for those who need it most.
The most reported change is social rather than academic, with break times becoming noisier and more interactive.
Ollie raises the life-skill objection; Rhodri answers that skills are taught in controlled settings, and Keisha wants explicit teaching rather than relying on the ban.
